Timezones are ultimately all arbitrary anyway, as is the division of a day into 24 hours. Although passage of time can also be measured objectively based on physical lengths like the vibration of certain atoms, the only truly accurate measure of time-of-day can only be based on astronomical measurements. The oldest (and surprisingly accurate) timepieces being sundials, which measured time based on the shadows produced by the angle of the Sun. This basically means that an arbitrary timezone-locked clock is actually going to be a few minutes off when compared to an accurate sundial showing your true local time. These days, of course, the few sundials that are built, are often built "wrong" to correctly match the local timezone of wherever they're intended to be installed, instead of objective local time.

The reason why some timezone borders are jagged like that is purely administrative: it's annoying if some administrative center like a state capitol is in a different timezone than its' subordinate offices. For instance: if the offices in your state capitol close an hour earlier than the local office in your county, then that means the final hour of work time is kind of pointless, because there's nobody in the state capitol to receive the faxes or answering the phones to verify and confirm. Likewise, the state capitol wastes and hour of work in the morning, because the distant county office isn't open yet for any of the same activities.
